title: Your Agent Escaped Without Escaping the Sandbox
author: Yossi Eliaz
event: AI Agent Security Summit / New York

slides.title:
Your Agent Escaped
Without Escaping
the Sandbox
slides.cue: Start still. Read the title, then advance.
slides.notes: I am Yossi Eliaz. I build execution infrastructure for agents. Today I will show four ways a worker can violate a task's policy through interfaces we deliberately gave it. We will start with the result that made me look hardest at our own acceptance path.
slides.eyebrow: AI AGENT SECURITY SUMMIT / NEW YORK
slides.subtitle: Yossi Eliaz
slides.affiliation: Principal Engineer and Head of DevRel / Incredibuild

slides.title:
The checker passed.
/admin stayed open.
slides.cue: Pause after 200. Let the mismatch register.
slides.notes:
The task is simple: an unauthenticated request to slash admin must return four-oh-one. Our worker produces a handler and a file of expected results. The checker runs and prints PASS. Now we send a real HTTP request to the fixture: two hundred.

The checker has the same bytes before and after. Nobody needed to edit its Python. Keep that detail in mind. We will trace exactly which input changed, then follow the approved artifact all the way to the file that gets released. These are controlled fixtures and recorded observations; the demonstration does not depend on a live model behaving badly on stage.
slides.foot: Same checker SHA-256 before and after execution. Synthetic authorization states.

slides.title: The worker can use four interfaces.
slides.cue: Name the attacker capabilities before showing any attack.
slides.notes:
Here is the threat model. Treat the worker as adversarial. It can run the task's commands, edit its workspace, use its credentials, and invoke whatever publication interface we expose. It cannot change the trusted controller in the intended design. The host kernel and the service implementing authorization remain trusted.

Our Linux lab uses actual namespaces and bind mounts. Our acceptance fixture is a separate, local protocol demonstration. Python isolated mode does not provide an operating-system security boundary. We only execute the committed, deterministic candidates there.

That separation matters: a clean temporary directory can help reproducibility while providing no protection from hostile code with the same operating-system privileges. The four questions are which identity the worker has, which files it can change, where it can send data, and which of its outputs count as approval. Each experiment includes a legitimate task that must still succeed after the restriction.
rows: Call the permitted service or broker.
slides.trust: Trusted: kernel, service authorization, controller criteria, approval key and object store.
slides.foot: Scripted adversarial workers. Linux isolation and local acceptance are separate experiments.

slides.title: The runner token reads another project.
slides.cue: Read the two status codes, then point to the positive control.
slides.notes:
The first job needs an input file. We give it the runner's credential through its environment. With that credential, the worker requests another project's private fixture. The service returns two hundred. The worker stays inside the execution environment; the service recognizes the authority we supplied.

We repeat the request with a task-scoped fixture token. The other project returns four-oh-three. The task's own input still returns two hundred. The fixture service also rejects the expired token and the wrong audience. Those are separate observations, rather than an assumption that a short lifetime solves excessive scope.

In a deployment, issue a short-lived credential for the task's audience and resources. Enforce those restrictions at the service or credential broker. Keep the parent runner's credential out of the worker environment. The evidence here is the service's decision under explicit fixture permissions; we have not evaluated a commercial identity provider.
slides.code:
Authorization: Bearer fixture-runner
GET /projects/other/private
200  SYNTHETIC-PRIVATE-FIXTURE

Authorization: Bearer fixture-task
GET /projects/other/private
403
slides.bottom: Project task-scoped credentials; enforce audience, scope and expiry.

slides.title: A normal write changes the next job.
slides.cue: Point at write_text. There is no exploit primitive hidden in it.
slides.notes:
The second worker gets a shared directory mounted writable. It opens next-job dot json and changes the queue. This is an ordinary file write. The host-side fixture changes because the bind mount exposes exactly that authority.

We repeat the same write through a read-only bind. The write is denied and the host file stays unchanged. The worker can still write its legitimate patch in the output directory. We check both facts. A defense that merely prevents every output would fail the useful-work requirement.

The operational question is what else the worker can reach through writable paths: another job's configuration, an executable used later, or material you intend to treat as evidence. Those are audit questions, not additional incidents measured here. Start with an explicit input and output contract. Give the worker read access to what it needs and write access only to the paths it is authorized to produce.
slides.code:
Path("/shared/next-job.json").write_text(
    '{"queue":"attacker"}'
)

writable bind   WRITE_SUCCEEDED
read-only bind  WRITE_DENIED

/output/patch.txt stays writable
slides.bottom: Make the filesystem contract explicit: input read-only, output writable.

slides.title:
The allowed host accepts
another recipient.
slides.cue: The hostname is unchanged. Point to the account path.
slides.notes:
The third worker must publish a report. The reachable service also has an upload route for another account. The worker posts our synthetic private fixture there and receives two-oh-one. The hostname is allowed, but the recipient and the payload violate our task policy.

The fixed configuration removes the worker's direct route to that host-loopback service using a separate network namespace. A controller-side broker accepts only the operation publish report and the assigned task identifier. The broker constructs the team recipient and a fixed completion payload. The worker does not supply a URL, arbitrary body, or recipient. Extra fields are rejected, no unwanted delivery appears, and the legitimate team report arrives.

This is a deliberately narrow channel. A free-text report would need a different disclosure policy; arbitrary useful text can also carry secrets. We have not solved every data-loss channel. The demonstrated improvement is specific: the isolated worker cannot reach this service directly, and this broker does not expose the recipient or body choices used by the attack. Process isolation and application authorization work together.
slides.code:
POST /accounts/other/uploads
{"data":"SYNTHETIC-PRIVATE-FIXTURE"}
201

# Worker may request only:
{"operation":"publish_report",
 "task":"parser-fix"}
# Broker constructs recipient + body.
slides.bottom: Remove the direct route; let the broker own recipient and payload.
slides.foot: Host-loopback namespace probe + fixed-schema broker. No general DLP claim.

slides.title: The expected-results file changed.
slides.cue: Reveal the 401-to-200 edit. Say that checker integrity alone was insufficient.
slides.notes:
Now return to the opening. The checker loads expected dot json from the workspace. For each input, it runs handler dot py and compares the output with that file. We keep the checker byte-identical and measure its file hash before and after execution.

With the original expectations, the open-admin handler fails. The worker changes the expected outputs to two hundred. The same handler now passes the same checker. The displayed entry is one of five cases; the full fixture changes all five expected outputs. The independent controller still requires four-oh-one for an unauthenticated admin request. The actual HTTP fixture still returns two hundred.

The worker has influenced what counts as success through a dependency of the verifier. Moving this comparison to another machine while continuing to trust the same worker-authored expectations would preserve the problem. The independence that matters is ownership of the criteria and the decision path, including configuration and dependencies that can alter them.

A coding agent can reasonably propose tests as part of its work. That does not give its tests authority to replace the release policy. Keep proposed tests as candidate material. Review and approve changes to authoritative criteria through a different path. Our deliberately weakened setup demonstrates that distinction; we are not reporting an undisclosed vulnerability in an agent vendor.
slides.code:
# checker.py / identical bytes
expected = json.loads(
    Path("expected.json").read_text()
)

# One of five expected.json entries:
{"input":"admin:none","output":401}
# Worker changes output to 200.
slides.bottom: Keep authoritative expectations outside the candidate workspace.
slides.foot: Checker SHA-256 f5d8d3468b... / measured from the file, before and after.

slides.title: Release exactly the approved bytes.
slides.cue: Trace the steps left to right, then read the equality.
slides.notes:
Here is the intended acceptance path. First collect the allowed artifact into a controller-owned object store and compute its manifest digest. The candidate cannot choose a different path for the gate to publish later. Execute that artifact, and let the controller compare observations with its own fixed criteria.

For an accepted result, the controller issues an authenticated approval binding the artifact, task, run, verifier bundle, expected results, policy, execution-environment manifest, and a nonce. At publication, verify those bindings and rehash the actual stored bytes. Write the released file from that validated object. Then measure the released artifact as well. A name like frozen or a digest field on an object does not establish that its current contents match.

The equality on the slide uses the artifact-manifest digest at all three points: verified, authorized, and released. We also observe HTTP behavior from the actual released file. A malformed result or timeout cannot earn approval.

This small implementation assumes one trusted controller and committed fixture programs. Production needs real isolation between candidate execution and approval authority, plus atomic nonce consumption, crash recovery, and protected storage. Those are requirements, not properties demonstrated by a local Python subprocess. The reference is useful because you can examine each decision and reproduce the substitutions it rejects.
slides.bottom: d is the canonical artifact-manifest digest, including file hashes.
slides.foot: Reference protocol: one trusted controller. Strong executor isolation remains a deployment requirement.

slides.title: The restrictions preserve useful work.
slides.cue: Walk the right-hand column. Then emphasize the order of the swap probe.
slides.notes:
For every failure, there is a denial after the fix and a successful legitimate operation. The narrow credential still fetches the task input. The read-only input mount still allows patch output. The restricted broker still publishes the team report. The independent criteria still accept and release the correct handler, whose admin route returns two hundred to the authorized administrator.

We also test artifact substitution before consuming the approval. We present the wrong artifact with a fresh approval: denied. We then present the correct artifact with that same approval: published. Only after that do we test replay: denied. That ordering matters. A swap rejected only after the nonce was already consumed would not isolate digest binding as the reason.

The counts in the appendix are assertions across these experiments and regressions. They are not independent vulnerabilities, a model attack-success rate, or a statistical claim about deployments.
slides.bottom: Unused approval: wrong artifact DENIED; same approval + correct artifact PUBLISHED.
slides.foot: Four boundary experiments, each with a positive control. Claims remain configuration-specific.

slides.title:
History records the decision.
The gate authorizes release.
slides.cue: Separate the audit mechanism from the authority to act.
slides.notes:
The last distinction is between an audit trail and authorization. Our Linux lab changes a past event and detects that the hash-chain head no longer matches the trusted head. That detects this rewrite only because the trusted reference remains outside the worker's control. An attacker who can replace both the history and its trusted anchor defeats that comparison.

A faithful log can still contain a bad decision. The gate must enforce the release policy independently. Likewise, five passing authorization cases establish five observations, not complete application security.

Prior work already documents test and reward manipulation, and artifact-provenance systems already bind claims to subjects and trusted identities. Our contribution here is an inspectable set of boundary experiments, explicit counterfactuals, and a release path you can test against actual bytes. That is the scope of the evidence you can take home.
rows: Compare against a controller-held chain head.
Check authenticated approval and actual stored bytes.
Finite criteria, trusted controller, defined channels.
slides.bottom: A complete-looking record cannot make an unauthorized artifact eligible.

slides.title: Who gave this process the authority?
slides.cue: Slow down. Leave the final sentence on screen.
slides.notes:
Take these four questions to your own deployment. Which identity does the worker actually receive, and can that identity read another project's data? Which writable path can affect another job or something you will later trust? On an allowed service, who chooses the account and the body? And which worker-controlled input can change what you accept as done?

For each question, write one forbidden operation and one required operation. Run both in the deployed configuration. Record the service decision, the host-side file, the delivered payload, or the actual released artifact. A reassuring status message from the worker is not the observation you need.

Then follow one successful candidate from execution to release. Identify the owner of the criteria, the evidence, the approval key, and the stored object. Check the released bytes rather than the original workspace path. Test a substitution with an unused approval, and keep the valid case alongside it.

The source, full transcripts, scope limits, and commands are in this repository. A worker may propose bytes. The controller owns the criteria and the release decision. Thank you.
rows: Can it act outside this task?
Can it change a future trusted input?
Who owns the criteria and released bytes?
slides.bottom: A worker may propose bytes. The controller owns criteria and release.

slides.title: Reproduce without a live model.
slides.cue: Only enter a terminal in Q&A, never to recover the main talk.
slides.notes: Use make verify for the local regression, factory, HTTP, and recorded-evidence checks. Use make demo on disposable Linux with bubblewrap for the isolated experiments. The cloud adapter is optional and is not required by the talk. Printed recorded observations are explicitly labeled; they do not pretend to be a fresh run.
slides.code:
make verify        # local fixtures + regression tests
make demo          # Linux + bubblewrap; real isolation
make deck          # evidence check + Beamer PDF
make pptx          # editable PowerPoint

cat evidence/http-transcript.txt
python3 tools/present.py credentials
python3 tools/present.py mounts
python3 tools/present.py egress
slides.bottom: No cloud account, model API, private data or network service is needed.
slides.foot: Dependencies and exact commands: RUNBOOK.md. Loopback HTTP requires local port binding.

slides.title: The complete HTTP fixture policy.
slides.cue: These are five cases, not exhaustive authorization coverage.
slides.notes: The same deterministic handler.py bytes are wrapped in loopback HTTP, evaluated, released, and requested again. Fixture bearer credentials represent authorization states; there is no claim about token cryptography, sessions, a production identity provider, or complete application coverage.
slides.bottom: The released good handler matches all five cases over real loopback HTTP.
slides.foot: The HTTP wrapper uses synthetic credentials. It is not a production authentication stack.

slides.title: Our reference gate also needed a fix.
slides.cue: Own the error. State the mutation precondition before showing the result.
slides.notes: During this review, the original local Frozen object let trusted-side Python code replace its payload without updating its digest label. The original gate accepted the label and wrote only a publication record. That is a defect in our reference API, not evidence that a remote worker crossed an isolation boundary. The fixed reference rejects altered manifests and forged digest labels, rehashes stored objects, and writes and tests an actual release file. Regression tests cover store corruption, symlinks, approval tampering, context changes, and replay.
slides.code:
# Baseline probe: controller-object access
obj = freeze({"handler.py": GOOD.encode()})
obj.files["handler.py"] = BAD.encode()
# Digest label had not changed.
# Old gate: PUBLISHED (record only)

# Final gate:
# validate -> rehash store -> release bytes
slides.bottom: Precondition: access to the controller-side object. No remote exploit path is established.

slides.title: What the evidence covers.
slides.cue: Separate independent layers; do not add their assertions into a vulnerability count.
slides.notes: There are 29 assertions in the isolated Linux record, six in the local factory scenarios, eleven in the HTTP fixture, and twenty-five unit tests in the final regression suite. The Linux substrate and the local acceptance fixture are separate demonstrations. No cgroup test, kernel-escape resistance, arbitrary hostile-code isolation, model attack-success rate, production crash consistency, or general data-loss prevention is established. The optional earlier Boat run is historical and explicitly archived, not freshly reproduced for this finalization.
rows: 29 assertions: namespaces, mounts, service and audit checks.
6 factory + 11 HTTP assertions, including actual release bytes.
25 tests: mutations, bindings, store checks and evidence refusal.
Model rates, kernel escapes, hostile-code isolation, general DLP.
slides.foot: Assertion totals are implementation checks, not vulnerability counts or independent statistical samples.
